content: Despite the well-documented risks associated with not breastfeeding, the rates of breastfeeding initiation remain relatively low in many high-income countries, particularly among women from lower-income groups. In lowand middle-income countries, many women do not adhere to the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations to initiate breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. This review is an update of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2005. The primary objective of this review was to identify and describe health promotion activities aimed at increasing the rates of breastfeeding initiation. Additionally, the review sought to evaluate the effectiveness of various breastfeeding promotion interventions in increasing the number of women who initiate breastfeeding, as well as those who initiate breastfeeding early (within the first hour after birth). The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth's Trials Register up to February 29, 2016. Reference lists of all obtained articles were also scanned. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with or without blinding, that assessed any breastfeeding promotion intervention in any population group, excluding women and infants with specific health problems. Two independent reviewers assessed the trial reports for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the quality of the trials. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted when necessary. Investigators were contacted to obtain missing information. The updated review included 28 trials involving 107,362 women across seven countries. However, five studies involving 3,124 women did not contribute outcome data and were excluded from the analyses. The methodological quality of the included trials was variable, with many studies showing a high or unclear risk of bias due to issues such as inadequate allocation concealment, lack of blinding in outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. Healthcare professional-led breastfeeding education and support versus standard care: The studies in this category compared interventions led by healthcare professionals, such as breastfeeding education and support during the prenatal and postpartum periods, with standard care. These interventions included promotional campaigns and counseling, all conducted in formal settings. Evidence from five trials involving 564 women suggested that healthcare professional-led breastfeeding education and support improved breastfeeding initiation rates compared to standard care (average risk ratio [RR] 1.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07 to 1.92; Tau² = 0.07, I² = 62%, low-quality evidence). However, the outcome of early initiation of breastfeeding (within one hour of birth) was not reported in these studies. The evidence was downgraded due to design limitations and heterogeneity. Non-healthcare professional-led breastfeeding education and support versus standard care: Evidence from eight trials involving 5,712 women indicated that interventions led by non-healthcare professionals, such as counselors and support groups, improved breastfeeding initiation rates compared to standard care (average RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.40; Tau² = 0.02, I² = 86%, low-quality evidence). However, in three trials involving 76,373 women, there was no clear difference between groups in the number of women practicing early initiation of breastfeeding (average RR 1.70, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.95; Tau² = 0.18, I² = 78%, very low-quality evidence). The evidence was downgraded due to design limitations, heterogeneity, and imprecision (wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect). Other comparisons: Other comparisons in the review examined breastfeeding initiation rates but found no clear differences between groups. These comparisons included: Combined healthcare professional-led education with peer support or community educator versus standard care (2 studies, 1,371 women) or attention control (1 study, 237 women). Breastfeeding education using multimedia tools (e.g., self-help manuals or videos) versus routine care (2 studies, 497 women). Early mother-infant contact versus standard care (2 studies, 309 women). Community-based breastfeeding groups versus no breastfeeding groups (1 study, 18,603 women). None of these comparisons reported data on early initiation of breastfeeding. Conclusions: This review found low-quality evidence suggesting that both healthcare professional-led breastfeeding education and non-healthcare professional-led counseling and peer support interventions can lead to modest improvements in the number of women initiating breastfeeding. Most of the trials were conducted in the United States among low-income women with diverse ethnic backgrounds and feeding intentions, which limits the generalizability of these findings to other settings. Future research should ideally be conducted in a variety of lowand high-income settings. Studies should include data on breastfeeding rates over different timeframes and evaluate the effectiveness of interventions initiated before conception or during pregnancy. These interventions could include well-defined health education programs, early and sustained mother-infant contact, and strategies to address societal barriers to breastfeeding, all with clearly defined outcome measures.
